tldr: We showed that a reconfigurable gripper using an active-surface thumb driven by a belt and only three motors can reliably grasp and place books in two completely different configurations—lying flat on a desktop and packed vertically on a shelf—without complex coordinated control.
hero_caption: Two representative book grasping demonstrations using the proposed gripper. Left: Grasping a flat-lying book on a desktop by pulling and bending it in-hand using the active surface. Right: Inserting the fingertips into gaps between vertically packed books on a shelf to create space, then extracting and grasping the target book.
overview:
For robotic hands, handling objects that are thin, easily deformed by external forces, and composed of multiple layers—such as paper and books—is an extremely challenging task. Conventional grippers have typically required highly precise finger-gait control to wedge fingertips into narrow gaps, or specialized mechanisms such as vacuum suction or electroadhesion. However, these rely heavily on surface smoothness and rigidity, and a single gripper could rarely adapt across different environmental configurations, such as lying flat on a desk versus tightly packed vertically on a shelf.

To address this, the authors proposed a three-finger gripper equipped with an active surface (a silicone-coated driven belt) on the thumb, combined with a passive compliance mechanism and a symmetrically rotating reconfigurable mechanism on the other two fingers. The clever part of this mechanism is that it eliminates complex finger gaiting or high-level coordination with the robot arm; simply running the thumb's belt in a fixed direction pulls the target object directly into the hand. What is more, the entire gripper requires only three actuators.

Furthermore, by constructing a contact mechanics model based on Euler-Bernoulli beam theory, the authors mathematically optimized the fingertip wedge angle and initial finger layout to ensure that books slide smoothly onto the fingers without slipping. Real-robot experiments demonstrated high success rates not only across four types of books with varying thicknesses and friction, but also on ultra-thin items such as 0.08 mm plastic film, fabric, and a mouse pad. The gripper was also shown to reliably perform long sequential "grasp-place" tasks, such as extracting a book from a shelf and placing it on a desk, or picking one up from a desk and pushing it back into a tight gap on a shelf.
contributions: Developed a gripper mechanism that combines a driven belt (active surface) on the thumb with two underactuated, reconfigurable fingers, handling both flat-lying and shelf-packed books using only three motors.

Established a simple grasping sequence that completes in-hand repositioning merely by setting an initial posture and running the belt, eliminating complex finger gaiting and precise arm-hand coordination.
Formulated the contact and deformation of multi-layered books using beam theory, deriving the optimal fingertip wedge angle (20 degrees) and initial opening distance that prevent slip failures.

Demonstrated on real hardware high-success-rate grasping of various books as well as ultra-thin objects such as 0.08 mm film, fabric, and paper, alongside continuous sequential grasp-place routines between shelves and desktops.

sections.heading: Why Is Grasping Books So Hard?: The Thin-Object Barrier and Everyday Diversity
sections.summary: Thin, deformable objects like books exhibit hard-to-predict behaviors when fingertips slide under their surfaces, exposing the versatility limits of conventional precision control and suction methods. This study proposes an approach that tackles both flat-lying and shelf-standing configurations found in daily environments by uniting an active surface with an underactuated mechanism.
sections.details:
Robotic grippers have seen widespread adoption in agricultural harvesting and tidying tasks, yet handling thin and easily deformed objects (where the thickness-to-length ratio is $h/l < 1/10$) remains difficult. Books in particular are not only prone to bending under external forces, but they also consist of separable layers called pages. Simply rubbing the surface can peel back only the cover or a few pages, making stable grasping of the entire object challenging.

Moreover, in settings like libraries and offices, books exist in two geometrically contrasting arrangements: lying flat on a desk, or standing tightly pressed against neighboring books on a shelf. Previous thin-object grasping methods tried to achieve fingertip scooping through dynamic models or large-scale reinforcement learning, but the control typically became exceptionally complex. Specialized grippers using suction cups or electroadhesion rely on surface smoothness and air impermeability, rendering them unusable on textured covers or book spines.

To overcome these hurdles, this paper introduces a novel three-finger gripper featuring a continuously rotating belt (active surface) on the thumb and wedge-shaped, passively sprung joints on the other two fingers. Because the surface drive of the thumb pulls the book inward without moving the robot arm or the other fingers, control inputs remain strictly sequential and remarkably simple, which is its greatest advantage.

sections.heading: Scoop, Suck, or Roll?: The Lineage of Thin-Object Manipulation
sections.summary: Grasping thin objects has been tackled through edge scooping, soft grippers, adhesion mechanisms, and active surfaces. However, almost no previous approach could handle multi-layer separation while adapting across multiple postures using simple mechanisms and control.
sections.details:
Prior research on handling thin, flexible objects can be broadly grouped into four categories based on their approach:

- Scooping / Prying motions: Pushing fingertips into the gap between the object and the tabletop. While methods model changing fingertip contact points or use tactile sensors (like GelSight) to maintain force closure during scooping, advanced coordination between the arm and fingers is indispensable.
- Soft grippers: Using passive deformation of compliant materials to absorb uncertainty. However, because they often rely on surface-pressing strategies, multi-layered objects like books suffer from the issue where only the top sheet of paper slides.
- Suction / Adhesion mechanisms: Vacuum cups and electroadhesion bypass finger gaiting altogether, but they require the target to be completely smooth and are ill-suited for objects with high bending stiffness such as books.
- Active surfaces: Integrating belts or rollers into fingertips to roll the object into the grasp. While existing studies pull in fabrics or pinch up surface folds between two opposing fingers, they assume excessive bending and cannot be applied to thicker books with high flexural rigidity. Additionally, earlier 1-DOF belt grippers required arm re-orientation during grasping.

This work sets itself apart by placing the belt exclusively on the thumb while using the remaining fingers as wedge-shaped receiving slopes, augmented by a reconfigurable mechanism that alters finger arrangement to support objects of different stiffnesses and postures without requiring arm repositioning.

sections.heading: Versatile with Only Three Motors: Clever Separation and Coupling
sections.summary: To achieve both desktop book pulling and shelf-packed book isolation and extraction, the gripper uses a belt on the thumb and independent symmetric rotation and open-close motions on the opposing fingers. Motor 1 reconfigures finger layout, Motor 2 controls opening and closing, and Motor 3 drives the belt, maximizing functionality with minimal degrees of freedom.
sections.details:
To handle both shelf and desktop scenarios, the authors devised the 3-DOF reconfigurable gripper shown in Figure F2, composed of one thumb and two opposing fingers.

III-A Task Analysis and Strategy
For flat-lying books, the active surface on the thumb pulls the book inward, sliding it onto the two passively tilting fingers before clamping it. For vertically standing books on a shelf, to prevent neighboring books from being dragged out by inter-book friction, the two fingers first insert into the gaps beside the target book to physically isolate it. The thumb belt then contacts the top edge of the book to draw it out before the fingers close.

III-B1 Underactuated Fingers
The base of the two fingers incorporates a four-bar parallel linkage, allowing them to clamp books symmetrically from both sides. The fingertips feature a wedge shape for easy gap insertion and are connected to the second joint via torsion springs to form underactuated joints. When pressed against a desk, they passively tilt under external force, naturally creating a ramp to scoop up the book.

III-B2 Active-Surface Thumb
An S3M timing belt runs along the inner side of the thumb, covered with a 1 mm thick silicone layer to maximize friction. Five idler pulleys are densely packed inside the belt loop, creating a firm, broad contact patch when pressing against a book.

III-B3 Transmission Mechanism
To independently control finger opening/closing and symmetric rotation (switching between grasping and isolation modes), a two-layer gear transmission is employed. The upper layer is a symmetric rotation mechanism based on planetary gearing (Motor 1), while the lower layer is an open-close mechanism driven by a lead screw and slider-crank (Motor 2). A sleeve structure connecting the slider and links ensures smooth reconfigurable rotation regardless of the finger opening position.

captions.F2: Exploded view and mechanical architecture of the proposed gripper. (a) Wedge-shaped fingertip with passive spring compliance and four-bar parallel linkage, (b) overall appearance, (c) thumb equipped with six pulleys and a silicone belt, (d) two-layer gear transmission system that mechanically decouples opening/closing from reconfigurable (symmetric rotation) motions.

sections.heading: Decoding Dual Motions Geometrically: Deriving Kinematic Models
sections.summary: The kinematics of the slider-crank parallel linkage for opening/closing and the planetary gear train for mode switching are formulated. This enables the spatial coordinates of the fingertips and thumb tip to be uniquely determined from slider displacement and gear rotation angles.
sections.details:
To accurately control and simulate the entire gripper motion, coordinate systems were defined for kinematic analysis. The origin frame $\{O\}$ is placed at the center of the gripper base, with local frames attached to each joint, the slider $\{H\}$, and fingertip tips $P, Q$.

The finger open-close angle $\theta_2$ is constrained by the slider displacement $h$, driven by the lead screw of Motor 2. By solving the closed-loop geometric equations of the linkage, an explicit formulation relating $\theta_2$ to $h$ is derived. Furthermore, thanks to the four-bar parallel linkage, the orientation of the fingertip link remains consistently parallel as the fingers open and close.

Meanwhile, the reconfigurable angle $\theta_1$ of the fingers is synchronized by planetary gear constraints so that the two fingers always rotate symmetrically at equal angles about the central base axis. Ultimately, by providing slider displacement $h$, reconfiguration angle $\theta_1$, and passive joint deflection angle $\theta_4$, the fingertip positions in the gripper frame, ${}^O\boldsymbol{p}_P$ and ${}^O\boldsymbol{p}_Q$, are fully determined. These geometric relationships form the foundation for establishing the initial grasp postures described in the next section.

sections.heading: Why a 20-Degree Fingertip?: Contact Mechanics and Parameter Optimization via Beam Theory
sections.summary: Initial grasping approaches for desktop and shelf books were systematized. Furthermore, the desktop repositioning process was formulated as an Euler-Bernoulli beam model, mechanically deriving the fingertip wedge angle (20 degrees) and initial finger spacing required for the thumb belt to pull books inward without slipping.
sections.details:
V-A Grasping Strategy Design
- Flat-lying books: The gripper pitch angle $\psi$ and finger opening angle $\theta_2$ are configured so that the thumb rests on the book while the two fingertips contact the tabletop flatly (Figure F4(a)). From this state, simply rotating the thumb belt allows the book to slide onto the fingertip ramp via its own weight and passive joint deflection.
- Shelf-packed books: The fingers rotate symmetrically from grasping mode to isolation mode, and with a gripper pitch angle of $\psi=0$, the fingertips are inserted straight into the book gaps like wedges (Figure F4(b)). After pushing adjacent books aside to shield inter-book friction, the thumb belt pulls only the target book outward before the fingers close to grasp it.

V-B Contact Mechanics and Structural Optimization
When repositioning a flat-lying book, the critical condition is ensuring that the thumb belt does not slip on the book surface (i.e., staying within the friction limit $F_{f2} \le \mu_2 F_2$). The process was divided into two quasi-static equilibrium phases: before touching the fingertips ($l' < s$) and after riding onto the fingertips where bending occurs ($l' \ge s$) (Figure F5).

Because of the book's small slenderness ratio, an Euler-Bernoulli beam model was used to formulate its bending moment. Since a book consists of multiple layers, its second moment of area $I_z$ was modeled not as a single rigid body, but as a laminated beam accounting for individual sheet thickness $h_{\text{paper}}$ ($I_z = \frac{b h_{\text{paper}}^3}{12} \cdot \frac{h}{h_{\text{paper}}}$). Solving the beam deflection curve and moment from boundary conditions yielded the required belt friction force $F_{f2}$.

The analysis revealed that as the fingertip wedge angle $\alpha$ increases, or as the initial thumb-fingertip distance $s$ decreases, the normal reaction force required to push the book upward grows, causing a sharp rise in required friction $F_{f2}$ and triggering slip failures. Balancing physical constraints with achievable operating bounds, the optimal fingertip angle was identified as $\alpha = 20^{\circ}$ with an initial separation distance of around $40\,\text{mm}$.

captions.F4: Grasping strategies of the proposed gripper. (a) Initial configuration when grasping a flat-lying book (definition of geometric parameters), (b) schematic of the isolation strategy for shelf-packed books, wedging fingertips into gaps to push neighbors aside and isolate friction while extracting only the target book.
captions.F5: Contact mechanics model during the desktop book repositioning process. (a) Pure translation phase before contacting fingertips, (b) bending phase after contacting fingertips, (c) distributed loads and boundary conditions in the Euler-Bernoulli beam model, (d) geometric approximations.

sections.heading: Real-Robot Validation: From Thick Books to 0.08 mm Film and Shelf Cycling
sections.summary: Mounted on a UR5e robotic arm, the prototype gripper underwent four experiments: desktop books, shelf-packed books, ultra-thin items, and extended grasp-place sequences. Despite operating under predominantly open-loop control without arm-finger dynamic coordination, it demonstrated exceptionally high grasping success rates and environmental adaptability.
sections.details:
A prototype gripper (aluminum core parts, 3D-printed housing, three DJI M2006 motors) was mounted on a UR5e arm for extensive evaluation.

VI-A Desktop Book Grasping Experiments
Four books of varying dimensions, weights, and friction coefficients (the thickest measuring 14 mm with a bending stiffness of $7.7 \times 10^{-3}\,\text{Nm}^2$) were tested over 20 trials each. Belt speed was set to $0.036\,\text{m/s}$ to preserve quasi-static conditions. The three thinner books achieved a 100% success rate. Only the thickest book experienced two failures (90% success rate) due to higher bending stiffness during fingertip climbing, confirming high overall reliability. Grasping was also tested approaching from the unbound "fore-edge" side (where pages easily fan open), achieving 100% success across all four books and validating robustness against multi-layer separation.

VI-B Shelf Book Grasping Experiments
Testing on tightly packed shelf books over 20 trials yielded a 0% failure rate during extraction and grasping once fingertip insertion succeeded, with only a few initial insertion failures caused by positional misalignment.

VI-C1 Extension to Ultra-Thin Objects
Plastic film (0.08 mm thick), felt fabric, A4 copy paper, and a mouse pad—materials with widely differing stiffness and friction—were placed flat on a desk and subjected to the exact same grasping sequence. Remarkably, all four objects were grasped without a single failure (100% success rate) (Figure F7).

VI-C2 Sequential Grasp-Place Tasks
Long-horizon round-trip tasks were executed: picking a book from a desk and inserting it into a shelf gap, and extracting a book from a shelf to place it on a desk (Figure F8). Conventional grippers struggle to release books deep into shelves because fingertips collide with adjacent books. Here, reversing the thumb belt without opening the fingers slides the book forward smoothly, enabling clean shelf storage.

captions.F6: Experimental book grasping sequences. (a) Desktop sequence: initial posture -> pressing -> belt-driven pulling (in-hand repositioning) -> parallel clamping, (b) shelf sequence: fingertip gap insertion -> extraction -> mode-reconfiguration grasping, (c) behavioral comparison during in-hand pulling across four books with different physical properties.
captions.F7: Desktop grasping experiments on ultra-thin and deformable objects. (a) 0.08 mm thick plastic film, (b) flexible felt fabric, (c) A4 copy paper, (d) high-friction mouse pad—all smoothly pulled in and grasped using the identical control sequence.
captions.F8: Continuous sequential "grasp-place" experiments for library automation scenarios. (a) Workflow of picking a flat-lying book from a desk and smoothly sliding it into a narrow shelf gap, (b) workflow of extracting a book from a shelf and neatly placing it back onto a desk.

sections.heading: Summary and What's Next: Active Surfaces Paving the Way for Simple Dexterity
sections.summary: This work demonstrates that uniting active surfaces, underactuated joints, and reconfigurable mechanisms dramatically simplifies thin- and layered-object grasping without complex control. It opens the door to replacing intricate multi-finger gaiting with mechanically active contact surfaces.
sections.details:
In conclusion, the paper underscores the fundamental benefits that active surfaces (driven belts) bring to thin-object manipulation. Eliminating finger gaiting and executing each action phase via simple, sequential commands offers tremendous advantages for real-world robotic deployment.

Furthermore, combining wedge-shaped fingertips with passive springs naturally absorbs and adapts to environmental contact forces, with beam-theory-based parameter optimization firmly underpinning that robustness.

For future work, the authors outline plans to integrate visual perception for fully autonomous book management, add active angle adjustment to the thumb to broaden compatible object sizes, and integrate active surfaces into individual fingers of multi-fingered dexterous hands for advanced manipulation tasks.

takeaways: Replacing complex finger-gait control with active-surface in-hand repositioning dramatically cuts down control degrees of freedom and task uncertainty for thin-object grasping.

Modeling book grasping as a laminated Euler-Bernoulli beam—accounting for individual paper sheet thickness rather than treating it as a single solid body—enables analytical optimization of fingertip angles and opening gaps that prevent slip limits from being exceeded.
Reconciling desktop flat-lying and shelf vertical-standing tasks using a planetary-gear symmetric reconfiguration mechanism achieves remarkable functional diversity with only three motors.
Reversing the active surface solves the notoriously difficult release action of inserting books into tight shelf gaps without needing fingertips to open outward.
limitations: Current experiments rely heavily on open-loop control without visual feedback; positional misalignments of just a few millimeters during shelf insertion can cause fingertips to collide with books and fail.
For books with extremely high bending stiffness (such as large volumes over 14 mm thick), the reaction force when climbing the fingertips can exceed the belt friction limit, leading to slip.

Because the thumb angle and belt normal force are not actively adjusted during operation, minor manual adjustments to the initial posture remain necessary for objects of drastically different sizes or weights.
